h1: SEO for staffing firms selling to HR heads, not to candidates
metaTitle: SEO for Staffing Companies: Employer-Side SEO
metaDescription: SEO for staffing companies in India. Build employer-facing pages on contract staffing, payroll and compliance so HR heads find you, not job seekers.
answer: A staffing company's website usually ranks for jobs and sells nothing, because candidate traffic outnumbers employer traffic by orders of magnitude and buys nothing. The fix is deliberate: optimise only the employer side — contract staffing, payroll outsourcing, compliance, industry-specific hiring — and stop reporting job-seeker sessions as pipeline.
takeaways: Job-seeker sessions will dominate your analytics and produce zero job orders. Separate the two audiences in reporting before you do anything else, or every decision you make afterwards is based on a number that lies.
Your buyer is an HR head, a plant manager or a procurement lead with a headcount problem and a compliance worry. They search for **services, not vacancies**.
Compliance content is the strongest authority asset in this industry. Contract labour regulation, statutory registrations and state-wise rules are exactly what your buyer is anxious about.
Publish how your commercial model works — percentage of CTC versus fixed per-head fee, and what sits inside it. You don't have to publish a rate to win the pricing query.
Industry pages beat service pages for conversion. `Contract staffing for retail` outperforms `contract staffing` because the buyer's problem is specific and your proof has to be too.

sections.h2: Two audiences, one website, and only one of them pays
body: Every staffing firm's site has the same architecture problem. Candidates arrive in enormous numbers because job queries have enormous volume. Employers arrive in small numbers because there are far fewer HR heads than job seekers. The analytics dashboard therefore describes a business you are not in.

It gets worse than a vanity problem. Once candidate content dominates the site — job listings, career advice, resume templates — Google's understanding of what the domain is about follows the content. You become a job site with a services page, and you start losing the employer queries you actually need.
The decision is to stop competing for candidate traffic on the marketing domain. Not because candidates don't matter to your delivery, but because the marketing site has one job.

callout.title: The report that hides the problem
callout.body: If your agency reports one organic traffic number, they are almost certainly reporting a candidate number and calling it growth. Ask for organic sessions split by section, and for enquiries split by type. A site that doubled traffic while employer enquiries stayed flat has not improved — it's just become a more popular place to look for a job.

sections.h2: How to separate the two without abandoning candidates
body: You still need candidates. The point is to stop the candidate side from setting the site's topical identity or polluting the measurement.
There's a spectrum here, and the right answer depends on how central candidate self-service is to your delivery model.
numbered: **Cleanest: move candidates off the marketing domain entirely.** A separate careers portal or an ATS-hosted job board. The marketing site becomes unambiguously employer-facing. You give up any organic candidate acquisition, which for most contract staffing firms sourcing through databases and referrals costs almost nothing.

**Middle path: a walled section.** Keep jobs under `/jobs/` with its own navigation, and keep it out of the main site's internal linking. Most staffing firms land here, and it works if the discipline holds.

**If you keep job listings indexable, manage them properly.** Expired postings must not stay live — see how we handle this on the [recruitment agency page](/seo-for/recruitment), where job expiry is the central problem.

**Split the measurement regardless of architecture.** Separate GA4 reports for the employer and candidate sections, separate conversion definitions, and a single headline number that only counts employer enquiries. If your dashboard can't do this, fix the dashboard before you fix the site.
**Split the conversion paths visibly.** 'Hire staff' and 'Find a job' as two distinct entry points above the fold. Ambiguity here sends HR heads into a job search and candidates into your sales form.

sections.h2: The service pages that actually get bought
body: Staffing buyers don't search for 'staffing'. They search for the specific arrangement they're trying to set up, and the vocabulary is precise. A single page called Services covering everything ranks for nothing and answers nobody.
Build one page per commercial arrangement, each written for the person who signs it.
bullets: **Contract staffing / temporary staffing.** Who's the principal employer, who's on whose rolls, how long the typical contract runs, what happens at conversion to permanent, and who carries statutory liability.

**Third-party payroll.** Frequently the highest-intent query in this industry and the least well served. What you process, the cut-off dates, how statutory contributions are handled, payslip access, and how a client exits.
**Payroll and labour law compliance.** Registrations, returns, registers, audits, inspection support. Buyers arrive here scared, which makes it the best-converting content on a staffing site.
**Recruitment process outsourcing.** Where it differs from contract staffing, what a dedicated recruiter pod costs to run, and what a realistic time-to-fill looks like for your sectors.
**Bulk and blue-collar hiring.** Volume, geography, attrition management, and how you source in tier-2 and tier-3 towns. Manufacturing and logistics buyers search this in plain language.
**Employer of record and PEO arrangements**, if you offer them. The query set here is distinct and often comes from foreign companies entering India, which makes it high-value.
**Statutory registers and documentation support** — dull, specific, and precisely what a plant HR manager types at 11pm before an inspection.

callout.title: Write for the person who gets blamed
callout.body: The HR manager buying contract staffing isn't optimising cost. They're avoiding a compliance failure that lands on their name. Pages that acknowledge that — what you take on, what stays theirs, what happens in an inspection — convert better than pages listing your years in business and your client logos.

sections.h2: Compliance content: the authority asset nobody else builds
body: Indian labour regulation is complicated, state-variable and genuinely worrying to the people responsible for it. That combination is the best content opportunity in staffing, and most firms ignore it because it's harder to write than a blog post about workplace culture.

The material writes itself from your own operations. The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act and its licensing and registration requirements. Provident fund and ESI applicability, contributions and returns. Shops and establishments registration, which differs by state and trips up every company opening a second office. The four labour codes and the state rules under them, whose implementation has been rolling and staggered rather than instant.

That last point needs care. Any page about the labour codes must carry a visible last-reviewed date and a note about the current implementation status, because a confidently wrong compliance page is worse for your reputation than no page at all. Say what is in force, what isn't yet, and when you last checked.
bullets: **One page per statute or obligation**, not a single 4,000-word 'labour law guide' that ranks for nothing in particular.

**State-wise pages where the rules genuinely differ** — shops and establishments, professional tax, minimum wage notifications. This is legitimate depth, not doorway pages, because the content is materially different per state.
**Downloadable checklists and register formats.** These earn links from HR communities without any outreach, and they're the natural place for a soft enquiry ask.

**Reviewed and dated by a named person**, ideally your compliance head with their credentials on the page. Regulatory content is exactly where Google's experience and expertise expectations bite hardest.

**Never publish statutory thresholds without a review date.** Wage ceilings and notifications get revised. A stale number quoted with confidence is the fastest way to lose an HR buyer's trust permanently.
**Link every compliance page down to the relevant service page.** Authority content that doesn't route to a commercial page is a library, not a marketing asset.

sections.h2: Industry pages, and the pricing question you should answer
body: `Contract staffing` is a generic query with generic competition. `Contract staffing for retail stores` or `manpower agency for warehouse operations` is a buyer describing their actual problem, and those pages close far better because your proof can be specific to them.
Build the four or five you genuinely serve, and refuse the rest. A staffing page for an industry you've never placed into is obvious to the buyer within one paragraph.

subs.h3: Industry pages worth building in India
bullets: **IT and GCC staffing** — contract-to-hire, offshore development centre ramp-ups, and the concentration of global capability centres in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune.
**BFSI** — field sales, collections and agency-channel hiring, where volume and attrition are the buyer's whole problem.
**Retail and QSR** — store staffing, and the seasonal ramp around the September-to-October festive period and end-of-season sales.
**Manufacturing and warehousing** — shop-floor and logistics manpower, where contract labour licensing is the buyer's primary anxiety.
**Healthcare and diagnostics** — credential verification, shift coverage, and the compliance overhead that comes with both.

subs.h3: How to handle the cost query without publishing a rate
body: Buyers search `staffing markup`, `contract staffing cost per employee` and `payroll outsourcing charges`. Most staffing sites answer with a contact form, which is why the answer currently belongs to a competitor's blog.

You don't need to publish a number to win the query. Publish the structure: whether you charge a percentage of CTC or a fixed per-head fee, what sits inside that fee — statutory contributions, insurance, payroll processing, compliance administration, replacement cover — and what genuinely moves it, such as headcount, geography, skill scarcity and contract length.

That page answers the buyer's real question, which is 'what am I paying for', and it pre-qualifies the enquiry. It also stops a procurement team comparing your quote against a competitor's on a basis that includes different things.

sections.h2: What we charge, and what the guarantee covers
body: Staffing SEO sits at ₹75,000 a month and up in our [pricing](/pricing), for the same reason [B2B SEO](/seo-for/b2b) generally does: the query volumes are small, so every page has to be right, and the compliance content needs a subject-matter expert's time rather than a generalist writer's. Smaller regional firms with a narrower service list can start at ₹40,000. Ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, and you keep every asset.

The baseline we freeze on day one is your trailing-90-day count of qualified employer enquiries from organic search — job orders, RFP invitations and genuine enquiries from companies, tracked in your CRM. Explicitly not sessions, and explicitly not anything from the candidate side. That's the number that makes this measurable at all, and agreeing it is usually the most useful conversation in the whole engagement.

Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position for a keyword, because nobody controls Google's index. Three clients a month is what makes that promise affordable rather than decorative.

callout.title: Small numbers, long cycles, honest expectations
callout.body: Employer-side staffing queries have low volume and long sales cycles — a contract staffing deal can take three to nine months from first enquiry to signed agreement. Ninety days is enough to move enquiries, not enough to close the revenue they produce. Set the baseline on qualified enquiries for that reason, and hold the revenue conversation at month nine.

faqs.q: Should a staffing company publish job listings on its main website?
faqs.a: Usually not on the marketing domain. Candidate traffic swamps employer traffic, shifts Google's understanding of what the site is about, and makes every report misleading. Move jobs to a separate careers portal or an ATS-hosted board, or wall them off under their own section with separate measurement.

faqs.q: What keywords should a staffing company target?
faqs.a: Employer-side service terms and their industry variants: contract staffing, temporary staffing, third-party payroll, payroll outsourcing, manpower supply, RPO, plus city and industry combinations like 'contract staffing for warehouses in Bhiwandi'. Add compliance queries — contract labour licensing, statutory registers, state-wise registration — which bring the buyer in early and worried.

faqs.q: Does compliance content actually generate staffing leads?
faqs.a: It generates trust, links and early-stage visibility, and it converts when it routes to a service page. The HR manager searching 'contract labour compliance checklist' is exactly your buyer, one step before they know they need you. Keep every such page dated, reviewed, and attributed to a named expert.

faqs.q: Should we publish our staffing markup on the website?
faqs.a: Publish the structure, not necessarily the rate. Explain whether you charge a percentage of CTC or a fixed per-head fee, what's included — statutory contributions, insurance, processing, compliance administration, replacement cover — and what changes it. That wins the pricing query and stops procurement comparing quotes that contain different things.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to produce job orders for a staffing firm?
faqs.a: Enquiries usually start moving in three to six months, because employer query volumes are low and the winnable pages are specific rather than competitive. Revenue lags further: contract staffing deals commonly take three to nine months from enquiry to signature. Judge the first two quarters on qualified employer enquiries, not on closed contracts.

faqs.q: Is SEO worth it for a staffing company when most business comes from referrals?
faqs.a: Often yes, but as a defensive and qualifying channel rather than a volume one. A referred buyer still searches your name and your service before the first call, and a site that answers their compliance and pricing questions shortens that call considerably. If you want volume from a small query pool, pair it with [performance marketing](/performance) rather than expecting SEO to carry both.
